events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?

events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. It defines a flow paradigm as a content-addressed, versioned description of an interaction context - which carriers (addressed delivery, shared object) and structural operators (fan-out, fan-in, feedback, n-party, select, forward, derive, merge) it uses, and how thirteen separately declared rule dimensions are set (discovery, observation, contribution, management, redistribution, history, time, disclosure timing, contributor visibility, admission basis, representation, object relations, ordering). A channel adopts exactly one paradigm version at any timepoint. Participation is recorded as separately addressable role bindings with a scope, a basis, a validity interval and the rule version they were granted under. Role acquisition is checked by composable predicates that answer one of four outcomes: satisfied, not satisfied, undeterminable, verifier error. Status. Draft. events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. events.excerpt: Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system

events.excerpt: Status: a design proposal for discussion. Nothing in this post is decided. Changes described here would need to go through governance with token holders’ approval. Dates are aims, not commitments. 1. Context Two complementary developments were proposed that could affect validators in the near future. The first is the move to Metanodes, described in a forum post by Adrian . Besides relay chain consensus, validators would take on node roles that the ecosystem currently funds separately, starting with collation and full nodes for Asset Hub and People Chain, potentially with further roles such as Bulletin Chain as opt-in. Over time, this could replace the separately funded RPC, collator and bootnode setups. For validators, it would mean more work per node and stronger hardware. The hardware requirements are published in the Polkadot docs. The second is a smaller active set. A forum post by Jan-Jan proposes reducing it step by step via three referenda, one week apart (600 → 500 → 400 → 320), with the aim of completing the reduction before the end of 2026. The first referendum has already been submitted. Each step would require Fellowship whitelisting and a token holder vote. Together, these developments call for recalibrating validator rewards. Validators who take on more work and run

events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: CometBFT v0.38.25 can’t read an ML-DSA public key. Its PubKeyFromProto knows Ed25519 and secp256k1, and its MaxSignatureSize is 64 bytes, while an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309. That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it.
